title: Where would you use caching and how would you invalidate it?
description: Learn to identify caching opportunities, choose the right invalidation strategy for each layer, and explain the trade-offs between consistency and performance.

data.text: Caching is one of the most effective ways to reduce latency and database load, but stale data is the price you pay. A good answer describes where to cache, what to cache, and—most importantly—when and how to invalidate it.
There are two families of invalidation: time-based and event-based. Time-based is simple but can serve stale data. Event-based keeps data fresh but requires more infrastructure.

data.title: Time-based (TTL)
items: Set an expiration time on every cached entry
Works well for data that changes infrequently or where eventual consistency is acceptable
Risk: users see stale data until TTL expires

data.title: Event-based (write-through / write-behind)
items: Update or delete the cache when the underlying data changes
Keeps cache fresh but couples write path to cache layer
Common pattern: publish a domain event, update cache in the subscriber

data.title: Cache invalidation is hard
data.text: Phil Karlton famously said there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. If you can avoid caching, that is often the simplest solution.

data.title: Product catalog cache
data.content: An e-commerce product page is expensive to compute because it joins product, inventory, pricing, and recommendations. You cache the final HTML fragment in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. When a product price changes, a domain event publishes and the cache entry is deleted so the next request rebuilds fresh data.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Match invalidation strategy to consistency requirements
Always have a fallback path when the cache is unavailable
